analysis.one_liner: Gives patients control over who can see their medical records and penalizes unauthorized disclosure.
analysis.headline: A patient medical-privacy bill sponsored by the Senate committee's own chairman drew bipartisan support and a hearing but never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The Health Care PIN Act would have given individuals the right to see, copy, and correct their own medical records, required anyone holding health information to safeguard it, and barred disclosure of a person's health information except with the person's authorization or in limited listed circumstances. It would have set criminal penalties of up to 10 years and $500,000 for knowingly misusing health information for commercial gain, allowed civil money penalties and private lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees, and required a separate written authorization before health data could be sold or used for marketing. The bill was introduced in March 1999 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which held a hearing in April 1999; no further action followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who has ever received health care. Individuals would gain the right to inspect and copy their records within 30 days, request corrections, receive notice of how their information is used, sign one authorization for treatment and payment uses, and a separate one for marketing or commercial uses. Violations could bring fines, criminal prosecution including debarment from federal health programs, and private lawsuits with compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals gain the right to inspect, copy, and request amendment of their own protected health information held by providers, health plans, employers, insurers, and schools, with written explanations and a statement of disagreement attached if a correction is refused [S2][S3].

Covered entities may not disclose health information except as the bill authorizes; selling, transferring, or using health information for commercial advantage requires a separate authorization, and payment-card transactions may only share the minimum information needed to process the payment [S2][S3].

The bill creates real consequences: up to $50,000 fines and 1 year in prison for wrongful disclosure, doubled penalties for repeat offenses, up to $500,000 and 10 years when done for commercial advantage or malicious harm, civil penalties up to $100,000 for a pattern of violations, debarment from federal health programs, and a private right of action with damages and attorney's fees [S2][S3].

Entities holding health information must post clear notices of their confidentiality practices, maintain administrative and technical safeguards, and keep a seven-year record of every disclosure they make [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans, insurers, employers offering health coverage, providers, schools, and universities would bear the cost of compliance: obtaining signed authorizations, building safeguards, posting notices, and keeping disclosure records for seven years. Law enforcement would face new limits on obtaining and using medical records, including a probable-cause requirement for subpoenas. These compliance costs would likely be passed on through premiums and prices, and patients giving up some data flow could slow some routine administrative processing.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts, with exceptions, any state law on health information privacy enacted after its effective date, which could block states from adopting stronger protections than the federal floor [S2][S3].

Employers offering a health plan must obtain a signed authorization as a condition of enrollment, and health plans must obtain one as a condition of enrolling individuals, so workers who need coverage effectively must sign away data-sharing for treatment, payment, and operations to join a plan [S3].

Federal and state law enforcement officers are shielded from personal liability for privacy violations unless they acted intentionally for commercial advantage, personal gain, or malicious harm, and parties are immune from common-law liability for any disclosure the act permits [S2][S3].

Compliance would be costly for providers and plans: safeguards, model notices, single and separate authorization forms, electronic disclosure standards, and seven-year records of every authorization and disclosure [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is real: enforceable rights to see and correct one's own medical record and serious penalties for selling or misusing health data, in exchange for meaningful compliance costs on the health system. The weak points are the preemption of future state privacy laws, which could freeze protections at the federal floor, and the enrollment-authorization structure, which lets employers and plans make broad data-sharing a condition of coverage. On balance the bill's benefits would flow to patients, but its design leaves some room for the entities holding the data to write the practical terms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which held one hearing in April 1999, and it never was reported out or voted on in either chamber before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeffords introduced the bill on March 10, 1999, together with Sen. Dodd, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The HELP Committee held a hearing on April 27, 1999, printed as S.Hrg. 106-64, but the bill was never reported to the Senate, and no House action appears in the record [S5].
The bill's only cosponsor was a Democrat, giving it a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor, yet the legislation died in committee [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans, insurers, employers, and any businesses trading in patient health data were better off, because no consent regime or penalty structure constrained their use of medical records; patients got no new federal privacy rights from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health plans, insurers, and data users

for.role: Senator (R-VT), sponsor and chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, held its only hearing on April 27, 1999

sides.party_line_note: A Republican chairman introduced the bill with one Democratic cosponsor; no votes were ever taken, so no party split appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would require enrollment authorizations, safeguards, disclosure accounting, and a separate authorization before data could be used for marketing, with civil and criminal penalties. Its death left health plans free to keep handling patient data under the existing patchwork [S3][S5].
Life insurers are covered entities under the bill and could not obtain health information without authorization, which would have complicated underwriting using medical records [S3].

Employers would have faced new duties as holders of employee health information but also gained the enrollment-authorization mechanism; the bill's death left employers outside a federal consent regime that would have restricted their access to employee health data [S3].
The bill declares FDA-compliant adverse-experience reports to be non-identifiable information and exempts compliant reporting from liability, a favorable carve-out [S3].
Providers would face authorization and recordkeeping duties, but the bill also shields them from common-law liability for any disclosure it permits [S3].

Commercial use or sale of health information would require a separate authorization, and re-identifying de-identified data would itself count as a violation, cutting off a market in patient data [S3].
